title: Held in the heart
hook: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it (Salok M9 57, ang 1429)
tomorrow: Saloks at the close of a reading

segments.voice: Yesterday: rahio, and your line: still there when it's cleared. What was the one thing you named that has stayed? Today, salok fifty-seven, the last of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks. Day six hundred eight.

Last words get remembered. An aunt's final sentence gets repeated at family gatherings for years. A letter's last line is the one people copy out and keep in a wallet. Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks come near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the fifty-seventh, his last, sits close to the final page. After all the saloks about passing, about chains, about friends who leave, what does he choose to say last? Not a warning. Not a complaint. A plain statement of what he's holding on to. Today: held in the heart.
screen: `LAST WORDS GET REMEMBERED.` → `THE FIFTY-SEVENTH SALOK.` → `WHAT HE CHOSE TO SAY LAST.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-seven, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Raam naam ur mai gahio: I have grasped the Name of the Lord in my heart. Ur is the heart, the chest, the place you'd press a hand to. Gahio is a grip word: seized, held tight, the way a climber holds a rope. Then: jaa kai sam nahee koi. Sam means equal. There is nothing equal to it. Nothing weighs the same. Raam here, as across Gurbani, is a name for the one God who pervades everything, not only the hero of the Ramayana. The second line, in paraphrase: remembering it, every trouble is erased, and the sight of You is granted. Sankat is a crisis, a tight spot. Daras is the sight of the beloved, the glimpse of God. Look at how the collection has moved. It started with the world as a dream and a wall of sand. It went through strength gone, chains, friends gone. Then the turn: the Name remains. And now the last word is personal: I have held it. Not the Name exists somewhere, but it is in my heart, gripped tight. Sikh tradition hears the whole set as the Guru's testimony near his martyrdom in Delhi, and this as its final line. Heard that way, this is a man about to lose everything the world can take, saying that the one thing he held couldn't be taken. Nothing equals it. Whatever the date of composition, that is how the tradition hears it.
screen: `UR: THE HEART. GAHIO: GRIPPED.` · `SAM NAHEE KOI: NOTHING EQUALS IT.` · `SANKAT ERASED, DARAS GRANTED.` · `FROM A DREAM TO I HAVE HELD IT.` · then, large: `NOTHING EQUALS IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one line in your heart. Choose one short line from the past few weeks, one that stayed with you: nothing stays, today or tomorrow, rahio. Or a single word, like Waheguru. Put a hand on your chest if you like. Say the line silently on each out-breath, gently, like holding a rope without strain. When your mind wanders, come back to the line. If you pray, the line can be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ur, the heart, the chest. Raam naam ur mai gahio: the Name gripped in the ur, and jaa kai sam nahee koi, nothing equals it.
Your line: nothing equals it. Keep the line you chose with you today, and say it once when you're in a tight spot. Day six hundred eight.

fork.setup: after fifty-six saloks about passing, chains and friends who left, the Guru has one line left. what does he say?
options: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it.
fork.reveal: the last word is personal testimony: the one thing the world couldn't take, gripped in the heart.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ur, the heart or chest; raam naam ur mai gahio, the Name gripped in the heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: held in the heart is a soft, sentimental phrase.
what it means: gripped tight, like a climber's rope, and nothing weighs the same.
what a scholar hears: gahio is a verb of seizing; sam means equal; the salok closes the Saloks Mahalla 9, followed in the Granth by the Mundavani.

Transliteration raam naam ur mai gahio jaa kai sam nahee koi / jih simrat sankat mitai daras tuhaaro hoi: confirm.
Claim that the saloks 'end the main body of the hymns' and that salok 57 is followed by the Mundavani: confirm phrasing (Salok M9 is followed by Mundavani M5 and Salok M5, then Raagmala).
